newsitem.title: BELGIUM: British VAT fuel cut may pose problems, EU says.
newsitem.headline: British VAT fuel cut may pose problems, EU says.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government's electoral pledge to cut VAT on fuel may meet European Commission opposition, a Commission spokeswoman said on Monday.
But everything would be done to avoid direct confrontation, she said.

"The spirit of the (EU's VAT) directive was to bring normal rates together. The fact you should reduce (VAT on fuel) goes against that objective," spokeswoman Betty Olivi told a news briefing in reply to questions.
Labour has promised to cut Value Added Tax on heating fuel to five percent from a current eight percent.
All EU countries except Britain tax fuel at their standard rate of VAT, which varies from a minimum of 15 percent in Germany and Luxembourg to a maximum 22 percent in Finland.
Britain won the right to apply a reduced rate, from its normal 17.5-percent level, because it had no indirect tax on fuel at the time VAT directive 77/388/EEC was agreed.
Olivi quoted EU commissioner in charge of taxation issues, Mario Monti, as telling the European Parliament recently that a further reduced VAT rate on fuel "could pose problems".
She said there had already been direct contacts between the two sides and these would continue.
"The Commission is ready to study with the British authorities the best solution (to the problem)," Olivi said.

But she left no doubt that the Commission would act if Britain violated the EU legislation. The Commission can start lengthy infraction proceedings against national governments that fail to respect Union-wide rules which culminate in the European Court of Justice if no compromise is found.
The Commission's declared objective is to further approximate VAT rates throughout the Union, as rate differences are seen to harm fair competition.

But it has so far failed to narrow the gap between the national standard rates. EU states also continue to have the right to charge reduced rates on an array of goods ranging from books, newspapers and medical equipment in most countries to children's clothing in Britain.
